title: How Swearing Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore why people swear, drawing on Tracy V. Wilson's article and other sources. They cover the debunked "poverty of vocabulary" hypothesis, gender differences in swearing (including Rebecca Lakoff's work on minced oaths), the distinction between curse words and swear words, and the split between deistic and visceral swears. They trace historical examples such as "bear," the F-word's origins, and "zounds," then discuss swearing as a substitute for crying and as a social signal. The hosts review legal issues around public cursing (Pennsylvania citations, a Michigan canoe case), and the brain science showing swear words are processed in emotional and motor regions rather than language areas, with aphasia and Tourette's coprolalia examples. They tour swear words across cultures (Quebec, Mandarin, Dutch, Scandinavia, Japan), discuss mother-insult hierarchies, and close with Pinker's functions of swearing. The episode ends with listener mail about a Canadian Senate filibuster and a Thanksgiving question.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and poverty of vocabulary myth
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the swearing topic, mention the show is kept G-rated, and discuss the debunked poverty of vocabulary hypothesis, which a 2016 study disproved.

segments.title: Swearing's universality and gender differences
segments.summary: Swearing is described as nearly universal, with survey figures for men and women. Rebecca Lakoff's 1970s work on minced oaths and the double standard for women who curse is discussed.

segments.title: Curse words vs swear words and word magic
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish curse words (hexes) from swear words (invoking deities). Swears are divided into deistic and visceral categories. Word magic is offered as an origin, with the bear etymology and the F-word's history.

segments.title: Swearing as a substitute for crying
segments.summary: A line of thought holds that swearing takes the place of crying as an instinctive pressure release. Geoffrey Nunberg's description of swear words as manifesting feelings is cited.

segments.title: Social signaling and offensiveness of swearing
segments.summary: Swearing can establish group identity, intimacy, and trust. The hosts recall a boss who swore in an early meeting. Rebecca Roach's argument that offensiveness comes from the speaker knowingly risking offense is discussed, along with the history of the term profanity.

segments.title: Mother insults and cross-cultural hierarchies
segments.summary: Insulting someone's mother is top of the hierarchy in many cultures. Examples include Bosnian, Albanian, Turkish, and Mandarin swears, along with workplace swearing statistics.

segments.title: Legal status of public cursing
segments.summary: Discussion of laws against public cursing: Pennsylvania citations, the Michigan canoeist case involving women and children, and FCC rules on broadcast profanity. Private organizations can also restrict language.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break before the brain segment.

segments.title: Brain processing of swear words
segments.summary: Swear words are processed in limbic and basal ganglia regions rather than language areas such as Wernicke's area. Stephen Pinker's fMRI studies and Stroop-style color tests show swears distract attention.

segments.title: Swearing in other cultures and aphasia
segments.summary: Examples of cultural swears: Quebec Catholic swears, Dutch cancer curse, Polish cholera, Scandinavian devil swears, Japanese baka. Aphasia patients retain swearing, and coprolalia in Tourette syndrome is discussed.

segments.title: Pinker's functions of swearing and parenting
segments.summary: Pinker's seven functions of swearing are covered, including cathartic and emphatic uses, along with the hosts' stories about kids repeating swears and teachers who curse.

segments.title: Listener mail: Canadian filibuster
segments.summary: Blake writes that a Canadian senator read his autobiography into the record during a late 1980s trade bill filibuster. A listener asks why Canadian Thanksgiving is in October, and the hosts give contact info.
